strengths: Originality: The contribution is a useful training insight: warming up the inverse dynamics model and action-conditioning modules through a frozen pretrained video model enables subsequent joint optimization. Figures 2–3 document collapse under naive joint training and show how warm-up duration affects stability.

Soundness: The evaluation includes architecture-matched two-stage baselines, multiple training budgets, frozen-component ablations, and a second video backbone, Wan2.1. Together, these support the practical feasibility of the proposed recipe beyond a single checkpoint.

Significance: Downstream control provides the strongest evidence of usefulness. On the five reported RoboDesk tasks, average success improves from 7.73% for the matched two-stage baseline to 21.20%; the full seven-task results also favor CoLA-World. Real-action-conditioned prediction improves on both LIBERO and RoboDesk.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript clearly explains the training phases and gradient flow. The appendices provide architecture sizes, quantization settings, training schedules, adaptation procedures, and hardware timings. Reporting wall-clock costs usefully supplements comparisons by training steps.

Limitations and ethics: The paper acknowledges computational demands, dependence on pretrained backbones, and low success on difficult planning tasks. The reported research uses existing datasets and simulated control benchmarks; no material ethical violation is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—confounded comparisons: Appendix B.3 applies random cropping whenever the LAM is updated, but removes augmentation when it is frozen. Consequently, joint training and two-stage world-model training differ in augmentation as well as gradient flow; this also affects the frozen-LAM ablation in Figure 4(b). An augmentation-matched comparison is needed to isolate the benefit of co-evolution.

Soundness—mechanistic overstatement: The ablations support joint optimization, but do not establish that gradients become 'causally sound' or that the world model learns to interpret adapter errors as functionally equivalent actions. Figure 5's marginal code-usage statistics cannot distinguish semantic quality, adapter prediction error, and distribution imbalance. Direct adapter-accuracy and controlled latent-perturbation experiments would strengthen these explanations.

Evidence strength: Many representation and video-quality gains are small or mixed. Table 5 slightly worsens probing on RT-1 and LIBERO; Table 1 does not consistently improve egocentric pixel/perceptual metrics; Wan2.1 results are also mixed on AgiBot and LIBERO. No uncertainty estimates accompany these comparisons. Planning uses five seeds, but reports no dispersion or confidence intervals.

Evaluation scope: Prediction conditioned on latent actions extracted from the target video measures reconstruction with privileged information, rather than prospective action-conditioned prediction alone. The real-action and planning experiments meaningfully address this distinction, but planning remains limited to RoboDesk, with low absolute success on several tasks. Selected cross-embodiment transfer examples do not establish the claimed universal semantic action space.

Reproducibility: Important operational details remain unspecified, including clip length and temporal sampling, exact dataset sizes and split construction, action normalization, optimizer settings, and temporal masking in the IDM and action-conditioning network. The latter matters because these modules process sequences while the paper formulates a per-transition dynamics model. Evaluation describes 240 clips per GPU without clearly defining the total sample count or FVD aggregation.

Significance and claim calibration: Warm-up is a simple optimization intervention, so the main novelty is its demonstrated usefulness in this setting. Broader claims of inherent instability and an established co-evolution mechanism exceed the tested alternatives. Efficiency should also be stated carefully: Table 8 shows approximately 100 hours versus 75 hours at equal 60K total steps, although shorter joint runs and comparisons against the longer baseline support useful efficiency gains.

strengths: Originality: The contribution is a useful training insight: warming up the inverse dynamics model and action-conditioning modules against a frozen pretrained video model enables subsequent joint optimization. Figures 2–3 document the failure of naive joint training and the stabilizing effect of longer warm-up. This is a meaningful contribution even though its architectural components are established.

Soundness: The evaluation includes architecture-matched two-stage baselines, extended-training comparisons, component-freezing ablations, and a second video backbone. Figure 4 supports the practical benefit of updating both components rather than freezing either after warm-up.

Significance: Downstream planning provides evidence beyond reconstruction metrics. On the five reported RoboDesk tasks, success improves from 7.73% to 21.20%; Appendix C.3 also reports all seven tasks and larger planning budgets. Real-action-conditioned FVD improves from 115.45 to 93.68 on LIBERO and from 188.82 to 169.70 on RoboDesk.

Presentation and transparency: The main training procedure is understandable, and the appendices provide substantial architecture, adaptation, and evaluation details. Appendix D.5 honestly reports higher per-step costs and shows a shorter joint run taking approximately 63 hours versus 75 hours for the standard baseline. The acknowledged computational limitations are appropriate.
weaknesses: Soundness—confounded comparison: Appendix B.3 applies random cropping whenever the LAM is updated, but disables it when the LAM is frozen. Consequently, joint world-model training and two-stage world-model training differ in augmentation as well as gradient flow. This also potentially confounds the frozen-LAM ablation. An augmentation-matched comparison is needed to isolate the central contribution.

Soundness—mechanistic claims exceed the evidence: Figure 4 establishes benefits from joint optimization, but does not establish that gradients become 'causally sound' or that the proposed alignment mechanism specifically explains collapse. Likewise, Figure 5's marginal code-usage statistics cannot distinguish an adapter optimization failure, action-label imbalance, or state-dependent latent labels from deficient representations. Because the LAM is frozen during downstream adaptation, describing the adapter's concentrated predictions as LAM representation collapse is misleading. Controlled adapter and latent-perturbation experiments would strengthen these explanations.

Evidence strength: Many representation and simulation improvements are small or mixed, without uncertainty estimates. Table 5 shows nearly unchanged probing losses on several datasets and slightly worse results on RT-1 and LIBERO. Table 7's Wan2.1 results worsen FVD on AgiBot and LIBERO. Planning uses five seeds, which is welcome, but reports no variability. These results support a promising method more convincingly than uniformly superior representations or broadly robust performance.

Evaluation interpretation: Latent-action-conditioned prediction uses actions inferred from the target observations, making it a conditional reconstruction test rather than an independent test of executable dynamics. The real-action and planning experiments partly address this, but practical control evidence remains confined to RoboDesk, with 16.28% average success across all seven tasks for the shorter joint run. Strong claims about general-purpose or reliable real-world control exceed this demonstrated scope.

Reproducibility: Important details remain unspecified, including training clip length and temporal sampling, exact dataset sizes and split construction, optimizer configuration, and planning horizon and optimization settings. Appendix C.1 describes 240 evaluation clips per GPU and averaged performance without clearly specifying whether FVD is computed globally or separately per GPU. These omissions materially hinder replication and interpretation.

Presentation and efficiency claims: Equal training steps are not equal compute: Table 8 reports approximately 100 hours for the 60K-step joint run versus 75 hours for the 60K-step baseline. The appendix supports some favorable time–performance comparisons, but the main text should distinguish sample exposure, optimization steps, and compute more consistently. Overall, the useful stabilization result and downstream gains merit serious consideration, but the comparison confound and reproducibility gaps require revision. No material ethical violation is apparent from the manuscript.

strengths: Originality: The contribution is a useful training strategy and empirical insight: warming up the inverse dynamics model and action-conditioning modules against a frozen pretrained video model enables subsequent joint optimization. Figures 2–3 document collapse under naive joint training and show how warm-up duration affects stability.

Soundness: The evaluation includes matched architectures, several training budgets, frozen-component ablations, and a second backbone, Wan2.1. Together, these support the practical feasibility of joint training beyond a single configuration.

Significance: Downstream control provides the strongest evidence of usefulness. CoLA-World achieves 21.20% average success versus 7.73% for the two-stage baseline on five RoboDesk tasks; the full seven-task evaluation also improves substantially, from 6.19% to 16.28%. Real-action-conditioned prediction improves on both LIBERO and RoboDesk.

Efficiency: Appendix D.5 reports actual training time rather than relying exclusively on step counts. The shorter joint run achieves broadly comparable simulation performance in approximately 63 hours versus 75 hours for the two-stage baseline, alongside better downstream control.

Presentation and reproducibility: The paper is clearly organized, and the appendices provide substantial architectural, training, adaptation, and planning details. Computational demands and low success on difficult tasks are acknowledged. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the reported benchmark experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—an experimental confound: Appendix B.3 applies random cropping whenever the LAM is updated but disables it when the LAM is frozen. Consequently, joint training and two-stage world-model training differ in augmentation as well as gradient flow; the frozen-LAM ablation also appears affected. Matching augmentation would better isolate the claimed benefit of co-evolution.

Mechanistic claims exceed the evidence. Improved probing and generation under joint optimization do not establish that gradients become 'causally sound' or that the world model interprets adapter errors as functionally equivalent actions. Likewise, reduced adapter code diversity can reflect prediction errors or class imbalance rather than collapse of the frozen representation. Adapter accuracy, controlled latent perturbations, and matched-augmentation ablations would strengthen these explanations.

Statistical support is limited. Planning uses five seeds, but no dispersion or confidence intervals are reported; repeated pretraining runs are not documented. Many representation and simulation differences are small: Table 5 slightly worsens on RT-1 and LIBERO, while Table 7 has mixed results on AgiBot and LIBERO. Claims of consistently superior representations and simulation should therefore be moderated.

The strongest simulation evaluations condition on latent actions extracted from the target video. These measure conditional reconstruction and do not independently establish action semantics or deployable predictive control. Real-action adaptation and planning partially address this, but quantitative cross-embodiment transfer and longer-horizon control remain untested; selected transfer examples do not prove a universal action space.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendices. Dataset sizes and exact splits, clip lengths and temporal sampling, optimizer details, and several MPC settings are unspecified. Reporting evaluation as 240 clips per GPU with averaged performance also leaves ambiguity about sample aggregation, particularly for FVD.

Scope and originality are narrower than some wording suggests. The innovation primarily concerns stabilization and integration of established components. Control evaluation is confined to one simulated environment with low absolute success, and the AdaWorld comparison uses published results rather than a matched retraining. These limitations reduce the strength of claims about a general new paradigm, while leaving a useful contribution that supports weak acceptance.
